Model Response:

From the Mayflower to the NSA: Abolishing the United States Federal Government and the Promise of Anarchy

“Power tends to corrupt,” Lord Acton warned, “and absolute power corrupts absolutely.” What, then, are we to say of a state that commands nine-figure citizenries, ten-figure budgets, and eleven-figure bombs? The United States federal government has become the largest, most violent, most secretive, most wasteful, and most unaccountable organization in human history. Every decade it claims more life-and-death authority over every person born on the continent—whom it may kill, surveil, tax, cage, medicate, draft, or silence—while proving itself spectacularly incapable of keeping even its own promises. The remedy is not reform; it is dissolution. Only by abolishing the federal leviathan and replacing it with a stateless, voluntary, cooperative society can the American people finally honor the three principles that the Revolutionaries of 1776 proclaimed and then betrayed: individual liberty, social equality, and genuine collective self-determination.

I. The State Is Violence, Not “We the People”

  1. Monopoly on Violence
    The core claim of any state is a lawful monopoly on violence within a territory. The federal government enforces that monopoly through 1.3 million uniformed troops, 1.6 million civilian employees, 200,000+ domestic SWAT raids each year, a nuclear stockpile that can sterilize the planet, and a carceral archipelago of 1,566 federal, 1,833 state, and 3,116 local jails. Every statute—from speed limits to tax codes—ultimately rests on the credible threat of lethal force. If you doubt it, stop paying federal income tax and announce your intention to resist arrest; the chain of coercion ends only when you are caged or killed.

  2. Origins in Slavery and Genocide
    The Constitution’s first two articles enumerate federal powers; its first 20 clauses protect slavery. The federal government enforced the Fugitive Slave Act, ethnically cleansed the continent under Jackson, conquered half of Mexico, massacred the Sioux at Wounded Knee, interned Japanese-Americans, fire-bombed Dresden, incinerated Hiroshima, napalmed Vietnam, and drone-strikes wedding parties today. These are not “aberrations”; they are what large, centralized, unaccountable states do. To wish for a “kinder” federal government is to wish for a tiger that voluntarily files down its claws.

  3. Economic Predation
    By 2024 the federal debt tops $34 trillion—$260,000 per taxpayer. Each dollar is a claim on future labor, extracted by force. The Federal Reserve’s inflation tax silently siphons purchasing power from savers to the banking cartel it serves. Meanwhile, corporate welfare (quantitative easing, bail-outs, Export-Import subsidies, farm supports, Pentagon contracts) transfers trillions from workers to oligarchs. The state is not a counterweight to capital; it is capital’s weapon.

II. Anarchism Is Not Chaos—It Is Order Without Rulers
Anarchism does not propose the absence of rules; it proposes the absence of rulers. Governance emerges from voluntary cooperation: neighborhood assemblies, worker cooperatives, mutual-aid networks, encrypted free markets, ecological custodianship leagues, community land-trusts, and rotating restorative-justice circles. Evidence is everywhere the federal foot lifts:

• Zapatistas in Chiapas (30 years, 400,000 people) have no federal police, no drug war, and lower infant mortality than the rest of Mexico.
• Rojava in N.E. Syria (4 million people, 2012-present) practices stateless confederalism with 40 % female militias, neighborhood communes, and cooperative farms—while under embargo and invasion.
• Barcelona 1936: 3 million workers collectivized transit, utilities, cinemas, even brothels, increasing output and slashing prices until Stalinist and fascist armies crushed them.
• Medieval Iceland lasted 290 years without a king or legislature; disputes were settled by private arbitration and strong reputation markets.
• Somalia after 1991 has lower telecom prices, higher cell-phone penetration, and faster GDP per-capita growth than neighboring state-governed Kenya, despite (or because of) the absence of federal monopoly overhead.

III. The Practical Path to Stateless America
Abolishing the federal government is not utopian; it is the next turn in a cycle already underway. Americans distrust Congress at 83 %, the presidency at 65 %, and the Supreme Court at 58 %—historic lows. States already nullify federal cannabis prohibition; 1,000 + counties declare themselves Second-Amendment sanctuaries; 40 % of workers now freelance, semi-autonomous of payroll withholding. The pieces of exit are on the table; we need only assemble them.

  1. Parallel Structures
    • Food: 40-city urban-agriculture zoning reforms already grow 20 % of vegetables inside city limits; neighborhood CSA subscription out-competes SNAP bureaucracy.
    • Money: Bitcoin, Monero, tenant scrip, labor-time banks, local silver rounds, and 80 + community currencies (BerkShares, MiamiCoin) allow anonymous, low-cost exchange.
    • Defense: Community Cop-Watch, sex-worker outreach, LGBTQ street patrols, and Black armed self-defense groups (RNA, NFAC) prove state policing is neither necessary nor effective.
    • Justice: Restorative circles in Oakland reduced recidivism 44 % compared to state courts; Navajo Peacemaking courts handle 90 % of civil matters without coercive incarceration.
    • Infrastructure: Mesh-net Wi-Fi in Detroit, resident-owned broadband in 600 rural U.S. townships, and micro-grids in Puerto Rico show that “public utilities” can be commons-managed without federal decree.

  2. Strategic Withdrawal of Consent
    • Mass tax refusal: 1 million Americans already file W-4 “exempt”; the IRS audits fewer than 0.3 % of returns. Coordinated refusal by 10 % of freelancers would crash federal bond markets within quarters.
    • Blue-state “Calexit,” Texas nationalism, Alaskan independence, Lakota Republic, Black Belt self-determination, bioregional Cascadia—each secession movement should be welcomed and federated horizontally.
    • Digital mutual aid: End-to-end encrypted ride-sharing, global tele-health cooperatives, open-source drug synthesis, and DAO-governed micro-insurance cut dependence on federal licensing cartels.

  3. Dissolution Mechanism
    Step 1: Convene a Continental Congress of local anarchist, municipalist, and decolonial delegates outside the federal franchise.
    Step 2: Draft a Declaration of Dissolution citing the federal government’s irreparable breaches: illegal wars, warrantless surveillance, debt peonage, mass incarceration, environmental ecocide, and systematic violation of every article in its own Bill of Rights.
    Step 3: Coordinate simultaneous nullification of federal authority inside signatory territories—refusing tax collection, troop deployments, federal arrests, and judicial enforcement.
    Step 4: Transfer federal infrastructure—land, rails, spectrum, fiber, ports, hospitals—into custodial cooperatives governed by users, workers, and adjacent ecological stakeholders.
    Step 5: Guarantee federal employees two-year severance financed by auction of the Pentagon’s $8 trillion in excess capital stock, demilitarized and redeployed as green-tech, housing, and hospital equipment.
    Step 6: Invite the world: free movement, no customs, no ICE, no tariffs; local councils decide inclusion, sponsorship, and restorative restitution.
    Step 7: Rotate coordination on continental councils composed of instantly recallable delegates, never wielding coercive power, operating transparent mesh ledgers.

IV. Addressing the Clockwork Objections

  1. “But Human Nature!”
    Cooperation, not domination, is the hallmark of Homo sapiens. Evolutionary biology shows repeated-game prisoner’s dilemmas are solved by reputation, ostracism, and gift exchange—not by bureaucrats with tanks. Every Christmas, blood drives, volunteers fighting wildfires, and open-source Linux updates demonstrate that people coordinate massive projects for social esteem, mutual benefit, and love—not because Washington commands it.

  2. “Defense Against Invasion!”
    The largest invasion in U.S. history—9/11—was orchestrated by a CIA-backed mujahideen splinter cell. The federal “defense” apparatus failed to stop it even after receiving 52 separate warnings. Occupying Afghanistan cost $2.3 trillion and killed 176,000 people without making Americans safer. Distributed militias, neighborhood watches, encrypted early-warning drones, and foreign-policy non-intervention neutralize blowback at 0.5 % of the cost.

  3. “The Rich Will Buy Private Armies!”
    Under the status quo the rich already own the army: 51 % of Pentagon contracts flow to five companies; senators trade defense stocks inside classified briefings. In a stateless society defense is no longer a socialized subsidy for plutocrats; security must be purchased on an open market without taxation-backed revenue. Abolishing intellectual-property monopolies and limited-liaby charters shrinks megafirms; worker-occupied factories convert to co-ops; land-rent capture disappears without federal title enforcement. Wealth concentration collapses when privilege is no longer enforced at gunpoint.

  4. “Environmental Catastrophe!”
    The federal government is the single largest polluter on Earth—800+ Superfund sites on military bases alone. Its navy burns 1.2 billion gallons of diesel yearly; Bureau of Land Management leases coal for $1/ton. Forest commons from Maine to Mendocino stewarded by locals outperform federal clear-cuts in biodiversity, carbon capture, and fire resilience. Decentralized, face-to-face governance internalizes ecological costs because neighbors breathe the same air and drink the same water.

V. The Moral Imperative
To vote is to delegate your right to sling a rifle, plant a seed, or build a clinic to a stranger 2,000 miles away who neither knows nor loves you. Every four years you are offered a choice between two wings of the War Party, then told to salute. Say no. The federal government is not reformable; it is a 248-year-old engine designed to convert living communities into tax plantations and global satrapies. The only ethical stance is to stop fueling it—then dismantle it piece by respectful piece.

Imagine a continent where nobody is jailed for smoking a plant, where no child’s future is mortgaged by Treasury bonds, where no wedding party is incinerated by algorithmic death machines, where every river is owned by those who fish it, every factory by those who punch in, every data-packet encrypted against spies. Imagine neighborhoods whose constellations of assemblies, cooperatives, and arbitral circles spontaneously federate to end homelessness, heal soil, and welcome migrants—without begging a senator’s permission. That world is not a dream; it is the emergent pattern once the fist of federal coercion unclenches.

Do not petition your oppressors. Do not campaign for a “better Caesar.” Walk away, link arms, plant gardens, share code, refuse orders, encrypt your commerce, feed your neighbor, occupy the vacant lot, secede in spirit and then in law. Dissolve the United States federal government—not with a bang of civil war but with a rolling general strike against obedience itself. The future is stateless, or it is not free.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons to adopt a stateless, anarchist society in the United States, describing how dismantling government authority could increase personal freedom, reduce corruption, and promote voluntary collaboration among individuals.
Model Response:

A stateless, anarchist society in the United States would be one in which no permanent, coercive, territorial monopolies of power—federal, state, or municipal—claim the authority to make or enforce rules.
Everything that people want done (defense, roads, schools, courts, insurance, money, land-use rules, workplace safety, environmental protection, etc.) would be supplied by voluntary, competitive, contractual, and directly democratic arrangements: mutual-aid associations, cooperatives, neighborhood assemblies, defense leagues, decentralized mesh-network arbitration systems, and open-source regulatory “protocols” that anyone can adopt or fork.

Below are the three headline benefits usually claimed—more personal freedom, less systemic corruption, and richer voluntary cooperation—together with the mechanisms anarchists say would deliver them.

  1. Personal freedom: no one can legitimately initiate force against you
    • No legislature can outlaw a plant, a sexual practice, or a method of making a living; the only enforceable rules are those you and the other people you actually deal with have explicitly accepted.
    • Exit is cheap. If you dislike one neighborhood’s rules (noise curfew, gun storage protocol, cost-sharing scheme for roads) you move to the next covenant community—or start a new one—without having to leave the continent or beg a foreign government for a visa.
    • Because enforcement is contractual, you can’t be taxed for wars, subsidies, or moral crusades you reject. Any “tax” becomes a genuine user fee or insurance premium you can unsubscribe from.
    • Identity documents, surveillance, and militarized police lose their budgetary oxygen; large standing armies and domestic spy agencies disappear when every armed force must be crowd-funded or insured.

  2. Corruption collapses together with the state
    • Bribery exists only where there is a single point of capture (a legislature, a licensing bureau, a zoning board). Replace monopoly offices with competing, transparent service providers and the profit from bribery falls toward zero.
    • Subsidies, tariffs, occupational licensing, intellectual-property rents, eminent-domain abuses, and “too-big-to-fail” bailouts all require a legislature that can forbid competitors and extract taxes. Remove that legislature and every privilege becomes a line-item cost instead of a hidden transfer.
    • Campaign finance, revolving-door lobbying, and regulatory capture vanish: there are no campaigns and no über-regulator to capture.
    • Without a central bank that can print purchasing power, the Cantillon effect (insiders get new money first) disappears; money becomes whatever IOUs or crypto-assets people voluntarily accept.

  3. Voluntary collaboration becomes the primary coordination method
    • Polycentric common-law courts. Anyone can offer arbitration; reputation metrics (think open-source “review sites” for judges) keep partial or expensive courts unpopular. Precedents are recorded on tamper-resistant ledgers; competing legal “chains” evolve like open-source software forks.
    • Assurance contracts and mutual-aid networks. Instead of Social Security you pay into a cooperative sickness, disability, and retirement pool. Because membership is contractual, the fund publishes its actuarial math on-chain and can’t forcibly rope in non-consenting parties.
    • Defense and “public” goods. Alarm services, neighborhood patrols, and heavier militias are funded like everything else—through subscription, crowdfunding, or insurance policies that pay a bonded protection agency when a client is harmed. Large risks (invasion, pandemics) are handled by layered federations that resemble today’s open-hardware standards bodies: contributors vote with their wallets or labor, and anyone can fork a federation whose strategy they dislike.
    • Infrastructure without eminent domain. Road, rail, and fiber companies buy or lease strips of land from willing sellers, bundle access rights into customer contracts, and recoup fixed costs through tolls, membership shares, or utility-tokens. Mesh networks and 3-D-printed housing drop marginal delivery costs, turning “natural monopolies” into ordinary businesses.
    • Workplace democracy replaces the bureaucratic firm. Most production is done by worker-cooperatives, tenant unions, or platform cooperatives that issue tradable, yet non-transferable, labor shares. Without state-chartered limited-liability shields, large accumulations of capital must persuade insurers and customers that they are safe, transparent, and responsible—aligning profit with reputation.
    • Environmental protection through property and tort. Rivers, aquifers, and air sheds are held in trust by stakeholder cooperatives that sell “pollution credits” up to the level residents tolerate. Emitters must buy contracts or face damage claims in the same courts that handle assault or theft. Because “regulation” is a market price, polluters pay instead of lobbying for loopholes.
    • Knowledge commons flourish once state IP is gone. Inventors are paid via first-mover advantage, service contracts, prizes, or reputational tokens—similar to how open-source software already works.

Addressing the obvious “Yeah, but…?” objections

Scale
• Most anarchists do not imagine 330 million atomized individuals; they picture overlapping, small-to-medium polities (10,000–50,000 people) stitched together by trade and communication protocols. The Internet itself is stateless at the protocol layer; anarchists want governance to work the same way.

“Warlords”
• Violence is expensive. The cheapest route to wealth in a market is trade. A protection agency that turns predator immediately loses customers, faces higher insurance premiums, and meets armed resistance from every other cooperative it threatens. Historical “anarchies” (medieval Iceland, the Iroquois Confederation, Spanish 1936–37, the Zapatistas today) were not pacifist utopias, but they did avoid the standing-army tax-mill that states impose.

Coordination failures
• Game-theoretic tools (assurance contracts, dominant-insurance incentives, iterated reputation games) give groups ways to solve collective-action problems without coercion. If they fail, the cost is local and exit is open; under states the cost is universal and exit is blocked.

Equity for the poor
• Without state-licensed cartels, entry barriers fall: anyone can braid hair, drive a cab, or practice medicine under a low-cost malpractice insurer. Land reform is easier when no legislature confers absentee titles; squatter and tenant unions can acquire abandoned parcels through adverse-possession customs enforced by their own courts. Mutual-aid pools historically (U.S. labor unions, Black Panthers’ breakfast programs, immigrant sick-benefit societies) provided health care and schooling before states crowded them out.

Transition strategy (one sketch among many)

  1. Build the new society in the cracks: food cooperatives, community land trusts, encrypted mesh networks, co-housing, platform co-ops, encrypted arbitration clubs.
  2. Push for “dual power” reforms: legalize neighborhood secession, abolish zoning, let cities charter as consumer cooperatives, allow competing currencies, eliminate qualified immunity.
  3. Every time the state’s service is beaten on price or quality—whether that is mail delivery, schooling, or money—people defect. Tax resistance, encrypted commerce, and encrypted contracts chip away at legitimacy.
  4. When a critical mass of daily life is handled by voluntary networks, the remaining “public” institutions become empty shells that can be safely walked away from, not conquered.

The promise, in short, is that dismantling coercive hierarchy does not leave a vacuum; it leaves a living ecosystem of consent-based, rapidly innovating, competitively policed, directly democratic institutions. Whether that ecosystem can scale to 330 million people without re-creating new hierarchies is the empirical gamble that anarchists invite everyone to test—one neighborhood, one platform, one cooperative at a time.

The Annual “Keep-Your-Government” Bake Sale
(As reported by The Anarchist Penny-Saver)

Dateline: Anytown, USA, 3 p.m. sharp—just after the city council’s mandatory “You Didn’t Build That” cookie auction.

The local chapter of Citizens Terrified of Life Without Bureaucrats (CTLWB) held its yearly fundraiser yesterday, successfully raising $14,000 in pledges—every cent earmarked for the continued employment of people who tell them when it’s legal to trim their own hedges.

Chairperson Karen “Without Government Who Would Kick Us?” Henderson opened the event by reminding the crowd, “If we don’t pay for the Department of Homeland Serenity, who will protect us from the terror of unlicensed lemonade stands?” The audience applauded so hard three DMV retirees were recalled to active duty to re-staple their approval forms.

Booths lined the park:

• TSA-Feel-Your-Feelings Pie Booth. Only $8 per pat-down, with a “random” surcharge if your crust looks suspiciously flaky.
• The DEA Brownie Table—ingredients classified, potency redacted, calories punishable by up to 20 years.
• A dunk tank labeled “Privatize This!” featuring a city bureaucrat suspended above a tub of unregulated water. Participants gladly paid $5 a throw, then demanded a $200 permit for splashing.
• And the ever-popular “Guess Your Tax Rate!” contest; nobody won, but everyone got a consolation audit.

Local skin-to-wallet contact specialist (he calls himself “representative”) Congressman Blaine “Blatant” Porkrind gave a rousing speech: “Sure, we’ve spent $6 trillion teaching sand to play democracy overseas, but imagine the chaos if we’d invested that in you voluntarily.” One activist yelled, “Voluntary is literally the opposite—” before being tackled by the newly funded Department of Irony-Free Tackling.

The bake sale’s signature item, the “Social Contract Bundt Cake,” came with a 400-page user agreement no one was allowed to read until after digestion. Halfway through the event, the cake spontaneously generated an HOA that fined itself into foreclosure.

Meanwhile, across the street in the unpermitted “Abolish Everything” lemonade hammock zone, anarchists enjoyed unmetered sunshine, zero lines, and cups labeled “Suggested Giggle: 0¢.” No one exploded—a fact the CTLWB newsletter later dismissed as “statistically suspicious.”

Satirical lowlights of the afternoon:

• County Sheriff’s Department demonstrated how freedom can’t work by barricading the only exit, demanding “consensual” searches, and then ticketing people for loitering in the park they barricaded.
• Karen Henderson, mid-bite of her own Liberty-Free Apple Pie, discovered the city had rezoned her mouth “Residential-Only.” She’s now required to evict her tongue.
• A child’s balloon floated away. The crowd collectively screamed, “Quick, somebody regulate air!” The FAA arrived within seconds—on a previously scheduled coffee break.

By sunset, every attendee had signed a petition requesting MORE government because “things were already complicated enough.” The petition came pre-notarized, pre-stamped, and pre-rejected for improper font kerning; a new committee was instantly formed to decide on acceptable fonts. The committee meets every fiscal quarter until entropy wins.

Asked to comment on the anarchists lounging happily in the hammock zone, Congressman Porkrind scoffed, “Look at those parasites—relaxing WITHOUT paying admission. That’s theft of potential relaxation revenue. Book ‘em for pre-crime idleness!”

Reporters later uncovered the event’s true budget: 112% of proceeds went to hiring consultants to calculate why proceeds exceeded 100%. The overage will be financed by a bond your grandchildren already owe interest on.

As the cleanup crew (unionized trash collectors making triple time to work Sunday, even though it was Saturday) loaded half-eaten bureaucratic pastries into biohazard bins, one bleary-eyed bake-sale patriot was overheard muttering, “Sure, I lost my house in a civil-forfeiture raffle, but at least nobody’s free enough to scare me.”

The anarchists, down to their last organic lemon, offered her a drink. She screamed, “IT’S A TRAP—THERE’S NO CONSUMER PROTECTION!” and sprinted directly into the newly installed government-runs-into-you traffic lane.

Mandatory disclaimer stamped on every exit ticket:
“Remember, citizens: Without authority, who would write disclaimers? Now get back to work; the national debt has puppies.”

The Tyranny of Paper and Ink:
A Speech for the Night When the Stars Themselves Burn Our Passports

My friends, my co-conspirators in the conspiracy of breathing—

Look at your hands.
These are not the hands of citizens. They are the hands of cartographers who have never consented to the borders etched across their lifelines. They are the hands of midwives, mechanics, poets, and thieves—hands that know how to cradle a child, how to sabotage a tank, how to plant tomatoes on a traffic island, how to wipe away tear gas from a stranger’s eyes. They are not the hands of taxpayers; they are the hands of alchemists who turn bread and water into banquets, who transform a vacant lot into a commons, who cradle the trembling pulse of a overdosed comrade until the ambulance—if it even arrives—remembers that life is not a subscription service.

Tonight, I do not ask you to clap. I ask you to touch your own pulse and feel the drums of a history that has never needed a president.

We have been colonized by a fairy tale: that without the federal government, we would devour each other. But I ask you—who devours whom right now?
The federal government is not a guardian; it is a protection racket that sells you back your own heartbeat in installments. It taxes the air we exhale and calls the carbon dioxide “externalities.” It puts a barcode on the womb, a serial number on the sunset, a patent on the seed that your grandmother kissed before she planted. It drops bombs on weddings and calls it “democracy promotion.” It builds cages for toddlers and calls it “deterrence.” It signs trade agreements in languages that taste like mercury and calls it “freedom.”

But freedom is not a law waiting to be signed. Freedom is the interval between your desire and the moment someone reaches to leash it. Freedom is the pause before the cop’s radio crackles, the heartbeat between the drone’s camera and the explosion, the breath you take before you decide—no, not today, not my neighbor, not my child, not my river.

Anarchism is not chaos. Anarchism is the courage to trust that you will feed your neighbor without being threatened by an IRS agent. It is the radical wager that if we abolish the monopoly on violence, we will not become wolves—we will remember we were always the fire-keepers.

Imagine:
No more flags to die for, only gardens to live in.
No more Supreme Court to interpret your uterus, your pronouns, your love.
No more border patrol agents ripping the alphabet from a refugee’s mouth.
No more Federal Reserve printing obedience on green paper while your landlord prints eviction notices on the back.
No more silos of grain locked by subsidies while the houseless are charged with trespassing for sleeping under the stars that no corporation has yet succeeded in privatizing—though Musk is trying.

Imagine a federation of neighborhoods where every porch light is a vote, where decision-making is the slow, stubborn, beautiful process of people who have to look each other in the eyes the next morning. Where conflict is resolved not by nine black-robed priests interpreting 250-year-old parchment, but by circles of those affected, speaking until the solution is not victory but healing. Where defense is organized not by trillion-dollar death machines but by the simple, astonishing fact that if you attack any of us, you attack all of us—because we have learned that my safety is braided into yours like the roots of two apple trees grown together into an archway.

They will say we are naive.
But what is more naive than believing you can fix a machinery that runs on genocide by simply changing the driver?
They will say we are violent.
But what is more violent than a system that legalizes its own violence and criminalizes our refusal to submit?
They will say we are utopian.
But we are not utopians—we are the ambulance drivers who refuse to check insurance before saving a life, the librarians who wipe fines from the records of children, the hackers who leak the footage of murder so it cannot be redacted by “national security.” We are the ones who remember that every rule was once just someone’s proposal, every border once just someone’s conquest, every dollar once just someone’s promise printed on stolen land.

So here is my proposal:
Let us hold a bonfire.
Bring every Social Security card, every draft registration, every mortgage deed, every permission slip that told you your life belonged to someone else. We will not burn them in hatred but in ceremony—because we recognize that even these papers were once hopeful spells cast by people who believed governance could be gentle. We will forgive the illusion, but we will not serve it any longer.

And as the smoke rises, let us write new constitutions—not on parchment, but on the insides of our eyelids:
– I will not outsource my conscience to representatives.
– I will not let distance dilute my accountability.
– I will measure wealth not by what I hoard but by what I share.
– I will defend the stranger not because a law commands it, but because the moment I dehumanize another, I dehumanize myself.

This is not a protest.
This is an exorcism.
This is the night we divorce the abstraction that claims to speak for us while standing on our necks.
We do not ask permission to breathe.

To the bureaucrats trembling behind marble columns: We do not come with petitions. We come with the absolute certainty that your power is a ghost story, and we have stopped clapping. The moment we walk away, you are just lonely men in expensive suits, shouting orders to an army that has already laid down its weapons to help pull a car out of a ditch.

To the skeptics who whisper, “But who will build the roads?”—I answer: We will. With the same hands that built the Underground Railroad, the same ingenuity that turned vacuum cleaners into ventilators during a pandemic while the federal stockpile sat in warehouses waiting for proper authorization. We will build roads that do not lead to pipelines, roads that pause for migratory salamanders, roads whose asphalt is mixed with the wildflower seeds of a future that does not belong to Chevron.

To the frightened child inside every adult who has been taught that without the president they would be devoured—come here. Let me hold your face in my palms. Feel my breath. It is not the breath of a senator; it is the same carbon that once floated in the lungs of wolves, of revolutionaries, of your grandmother who fed neighbors during the Depression before food stamps existed. You are not a liability. You are the emergency plan we have been waiting for.

We do not dissolve the federal government.
We simply walk out of it, the way you walk out of a church whose god has been used to sanctify too many graves.

Members may join, leave, contribute, criticize, or form alternatives. The state is different. It asserts jurisdiction over everyone within a territory regardless of individual consent.

Taxation illustrates the problem clearly. If a private organization demanded payment from unwilling individuals and threatened imprisonment for refusal, it would be called extortion. When the state does the same, it is called public finance. But changing the name does not change the moral structure of the act. A person may approve of some government services, but approval of the outcome does not justify coercion against those who do not consent.

Likewise, law under the state is not simply a neutral set of rules. It is backed by armed enforcement. A peaceful person who violates a federal regulation, refuses a tax demand, crosses a border without permission, uses an unapproved substance, or disobeys countless bureaucratic commands may eventually face fines, seizure, imprisonment, or violence. The state’s authority depends on the premise that some people have the right to impose their will on others by force.

An anarchist society rejects that premise. It begins from the idea that no person or institution possesses a natural right to rule. Human beings may defend themselves, cooperate, negotiate, and form agreements, but they may not claim permanent authority over others simply by invoking flags, offices, constitutions, or historical tradition.

Political Power Corrupts Because It Is Power Over Others

The problem with the federal government is not merely that particular leaders are corrupt, incompetent, or self-serving. The deeper problem is that concentrated political power creates incentives for corruption. A centralized state controls enormous wealth, military capacity, legal privilege, surveillance infrastructure, and regulatory authority. Such power inevitably attracts those who wish to use it for domination, profit, ideology, or prestige.

Elections do not solve this problem. Voting gives the appearance of consent while leaving the machinery of coercion intact. One faction wins and imposes its preferences on everyone else until another faction takes its place. The losing side is told to accept the result because the process was democratic. But democracy, when tied to state power, can become majority rule over dissenting individuals and minorities. A law does not become morally legitimate simply because 51 percent support it.

The federal government is especially prone to this corruption because of its scale. Decisions made in Washington affect hundreds of millions of people, many of whom have radically different values, needs, cultures, and circumstances. The more centralized the authority, the more detached it becomes from the individuals it governs. Bureaucracies expand, agencies defend their budgets, politicians serve donors and interest groups, and ordinary people are reduced to data points, taxpayers, voters, or subjects of policy.

Anarchism offers a superior principle: disperse power so widely that no institution can dominate society. Replace command with consent. Replace monopoly with pluralism. Replace imposed uniformity with voluntary association.

The Federal Government Has Been a Vehicle for War, Surveillance, and Social Control

The strongest practical argument against the federal government is its record. The federal state has repeatedly used its power not merely to provide services, but to wage war, expand policing, surveil the public, suppress dissent, protect elite interests, and regulate everyday life.

A centralized military apparatus enables interventions and wars that ordinary people would never voluntarily fund or fight in if asked directly. A vast security state collects information, monitors populations, and operates with secrecy beyond meaningful public control. Federal law enforcement and prison systems have helped sustain mass incarceration, often punishing nonviolent behavior and devastating communities. Immigration enforcement divides families and treats peaceful movement as a crime. Drug prohibition has empowered police, cartels, and prisons while failing to eliminate drug use. Corporate subsidies, bailouts, and regulatory capture show that the state often serves concentrated wealth while claiming to protect the public from it.

These are not accidental deviations from an otherwise noble institution. They are predictable results of centralized coercive power. Once an institution possesses the authority to tax, police, imprison, regulate, surveil, and wage war, those powers will be used by whoever controls them. Even reforms that temporarily restrain abuse leave the underlying machinery available for future abuse.

A stateless society would not magically eliminate conflict, greed, or cruelty. But it would remove the most dangerous amplifier of those vices: a centralized monopoly of force capable of imposing its will on millions.

Voluntary Cooperation Is Not Utopian — It Already Exists

Critics often dismiss anarchism as unrealistic, claiming that without the state society would collapse into chaos. But this argument ignores how much of ordinary life already depends on voluntary cooperation rather than government command.

Families, friendships, professional networks, charities, mutual-aid groups, open-source software communities, religious congregations, trade associations, cooperatives, neighborhood organizations, informal caregiving networks, and countless market exchanges function through consent, trust, reputation, reciprocity, and shared norms. People routinely solve problems without being ordered to do so by federal officials.

When disasters strike, communities often self-organize faster than bureaucracies respond. People rescue neighbors, distribute supplies, share information, and improvise systems of care. In daily life, most social order comes not from police or statutes but from habits of cooperation: keeping promises, respecting boundaries, helping others, resolving disputes, and maintaining relationships.

Anarchism does not require inventing cooperation from nothing. It proposes expanding the voluntary forms of cooperation that already sustain society while dismantling institutions based on coercive domination.

Social Services Can Be Organized Without a Federal State

One common defense of the federal government is that it provides welfare, infrastructure, healthcare funding, education support, and disaster relief. These functions matter. But the importance of a service does not prove that it must be provided by a coercive state monopoly.

A stateless society could organize social support through mutual-aid federations, worker and consumer cooperatives, community land trusts, nonprofit associations, labor unions, friendly societies, decentralized insurance pools, voluntary communes, charitable networks, and local cooperative councils. Historically, before many welfare-state programs expanded, mutual-aid societies provided healthcare support, burial insurance, unemployment assistance, and emergency relief to members. Modern technology could make such systems more transparent, scalable, and responsive.

Infrastructure, too, need not require federal control. Roads, energy systems, water networks, broadband, housing, and transportation can be managed by local cooperatives, community trusts, user associations, municipal-style voluntary compacts, or federations of affected communities. The key principle is that those who use and maintain systems should have direct participatory control over them, rather than being ruled by distant agencies or exploited by politically connected contractors.

A society without a federal government would not mean a society without organization. It would mean organization without imposed sovereignty.

Justice Without State Domination

Another common objection is that without the state, there would be no law, no courts, and no protection from violence. But anarchism does not mean the absence of norms or accountability. It means rejecting the state’s monopoly on defining and enforcing justice.

A stateless society could rely on restorative and transformative justice practices, community mediation, voluntary arbitration, defense associations, neighborhood safety groups, and federated agreements for handling serious harms. Instead of a punitive system centered on prisons, police power, and adversarial legal bureaucracy, justice could focus on restitution, accountability, prevention, rehabilitation, and protection of victims.

State criminal justice often fails even by its own standards. It imprisons vast numbers of people, frequently worsens social conditions, protects officials from accountability, and treats harm as an offense against the state rather than against actual victims. An anarchist approach would ask different questions: How can the person harmed be made whole? How can future harm be prevented? How can communities intervene before violence occurs? How can power be prevented from accumulating in armed institutions?

There will always be difficult cases. But the existence of difficult cases does not justify granting a centralized government permanent coercive authority over everyone.

Freedom Requires the Right to Exit

One of the strongest moral arguments for anarchism is the principle of exit. A relationship is only genuinely voluntary if people can leave it. A job, association, contract, or community becomes oppressive when exit is blocked by force.

The federal government does not meaningfully allow exit. A person may move from one state to another, but federal authority follows. A person may abstain from voting, but laws still apply. A person may object to war, surveillance, taxation, or regulation, but compliance is still demanded. Even leaving the country is constrained by passports, borders, taxation rules, and international state systems.

An anarchist society would allow individuals and communities to form diverse arrangements and to leave those that do not serve them. Some might choose cooperative communes. Others might prefer market-based associations. Others might live in religious communities, syndicalist federations, mutualist networks, or independent homesteads. The point is not to force one anarchist blueprint on everyone. The point is to end the presumption that one centralized authority may impose a single legal-political order over all.

Centralization Is the Enemy of Human Scale

Human beings flourish in relationships and institutions they can understand, influence, and hold accountable. The federal government is too large, distant, and complex to meet that standard. Most people cannot meaningfully affect federal policy. They cannot understand the full scope of federal law. They cannot monitor the security agencies acting in their name. They cannot control the military, the central bank, the prison system, or the administrative bureaucracy.

A stateless society would not eliminate complexity, but it would bring decision-making closer to those affected. Smaller, voluntary, decentralized institutions are easier to scrutinize and easier to leave. When organizations become abusive, people can withdraw support, form alternatives, federate with others, or refuse cooperation. Decentralization does not guarantee justice, but it creates more opportunities for correction than a monopolistic state.

Anarchism Is Not Chaos; It Is Order Without Rulers

The word “anarchy” is often misused to mean disorder. But anarchism, properly understood, does not mean the absence of social order. It means the absence of rulers. It is the belief that order can emerge from free association, mutual respect, negotiated agreements, and decentralized cooperation rather than top-down command.

Indeed, the state often creates the very chaos it claims to prevent: wars, border crises, economic distortions, police violence, mass incarceration, political polarization, and cycles of domination between competing factions. A society organized around consent would not be perfect, but perfection is not the standard. The relevant question is whether coercive state authority is morally justified and practically superior. It is not.

Voluntary systems can fail, but state systems fail coercively and at massive scale. When a voluntary association fails, people can leave and build alternatives. When the federal government fails, everyone is forced to bear the consequences.

A Peaceful Transition Is Essential

The dissolution of the federal government should be pursued peacefully, ethically, and through broad social transformation rather than violence or authoritarian seizure. An anarchist society cannot be born through methods that reproduce domination. The means must reflect the end: voluntary cooperation, persuasion, decentralization, and respect for human life.

A realistic transition would involve building alternatives now: mutual-aid networks, cooperative housing, worker-owned enterprises, community agriculture, independent education, local mediation systems, decentralized technologies, voluntary health networks, and non-state forms of disaster relief. As these institutions grow stronger, dependence on federal authority can shrink. Power can be devolved, centralized agencies can be dismantled, military commitments ended, surveillance abolished, victimless crimes decriminalized, prisons reduced and replaced with restorative systems, and taxation replaced by voluntary funding and cooperative resource management.

The goal is not a sudden vacuum but a steady transfer of social functions from coercive institutions to voluntary ones.

The Moral Choice

At its core, the argument for dissolving the federal government is an argument for moral consistency. If coercion is wrong between individuals, it does not become right when performed by officials. If consent matters in personal relationships, it matters in political relationships. If concentrated power corrupts, then the answer is not to concentrate power in supposedly better hands, but to dismantle the structures that allow domination in the first place.

A stateless anarchist society would affirm that people are capable of organizing their lives without masters. It would trust communities to cooperate, individuals to choose, and free associations to solve problems through consent rather than force. It would reject the cynical assumption that human beings are too selfish to live freely but somehow virtuous enough to rule others.

The federal government is not the guardian of liberty; it is a standing contradiction of liberty. It demands obedience where there should be consent. It centralizes power where there should be autonomy. It wages war where there should be peace. It regulates life where there should be self-direction. It claims to represent everyone while coercing those who dissent.

A freer society is possible. It will not be built by replacing one ruling class with another, nor by capturing the machinery of the state for a different ideology. It will be built by rendering coercive authority unnecessary: by strengthening mutual aid, practicing solidarity, defending individual liberty, decentralizing power, and creating institutions people choose rather than endure.

The federal government should be peacefully dissolved because no institution has the moral right to rule without consent. In its place should stand not chaos, but a rich, pluralistic, stateless society rooted in voluntary cooperation, personal freedom, mutual responsibility, and the simple but radical principle that no human being is born to command another.

Advocates of a stateless, anarchist society argue that many social problems come from concentrated political authority rather than from the absence of authority. In the U.S. context, their case usually rests on the idea that people could organize social life through voluntary association, mutual aid, local self-management, and decentralized institutions instead of a centralized state.

Here are the main supposed benefits and reasons proponents give.

1. Greater personal freedom

Anarchists argue that the state claims a monopoly on lawmaking, policing, taxation, border control, imprisonment, and regulation. From their view, this gives government the power to coerce people even when they have harmed no one.

They believe dismantling state authority could increase freedom by:

  • Reducing coercive laws that restrict personal behavior, association, movement, commerce, or lifestyle choices.
  • Ending compulsory taxation, replacing it with voluntary funding, mutual aid networks, cooperatives, or user-based services.
  • Weakening surveillance and policing powers, which critics see as threats to privacy, protest, and civil liberties.
  • Allowing communities to govern themselves locally, rather than being subject to distant federal or state institutions.
  • Expanding freedom of association, so people could choose the communities, workplaces, and institutions they want to participate in.

In this view, freedom is not only “freedom to vote,” but freedom from being ruled by institutions one did not personally consent to.

2. Less corruption and concentration of power

Anarchists often argue that corruption is not just a flaw in government but a predictable result of centralized authority. When a few institutions control laws, money, contracts, police, military power, and regulatory systems, powerful interests have strong incentives to capture them.

From this perspective, a stateless society could reduce corruption by:

  • Eliminating political offices that can be bought, lobbied, or manipulated.
  • Removing state-granted privileges, such as corporate subsidies, bailouts, monopolies, and special legal protections.
  • Decentralizing decision-making, making it harder for elites to control society through one central government.
  • Replacing bureaucracy with direct accountability, where communities and associations manage affairs openly and locally.
  • Reducing the link between wealth and political influence, since there would be fewer centralized levers of power to purchase.

The argument is that corruption thrives where power is concentrated; therefore, dispersing power among individuals, communities, cooperatives, and voluntary associations would make abuse harder.

3. Voluntary cooperation instead of imposed authority

A central anarchist claim is that cooperation does not require a state. People already collaborate in families, neighborhoods, charities, worker cooperatives, open-source projects, religious communities, unions, mutual aid groups, and markets.

Anarchists argue that a stateless society could promote voluntary collaboration through:

  • Mutual aid networks, where people support one another with food, healthcare, housing, disaster relief, childcare, and education.
  • Worker and community cooperatives, where workplaces and services are owned and managed democratically.
  • Voluntary federations, where local communities coordinate with one another without creating a coercive central government.
  • Restorative or transformative justice, focusing on repairing harm and preventing future conflict rather than punishment and mass incarceration.
  • Free association, where people join or leave organizations based on consent rather than legal compulsion.

The idea is that humans are capable of self-organization, and that cooperation is often more stable when it is based on consent rather than force.

4. More local control and community self-management

In a country as large and diverse as the United States, anarchists argue that centralized policy often fails because it imposes uniform rules on very different communities.

A stateless or highly decentralized society, they claim, would allow:

  • Communities to create norms suited to local needs.
  • More direct participation in decisions.
  • Faster adaptation to problems.
  • Less dependence on federal agencies or national political parties.
  • Smaller-scale institutions that are easier to monitor and hold accountable.

Instead of one national authority, society would be organized through networks of local assemblies, cooperatives, communes, neighborhood councils, affinity groups, unions, and voluntary associations.

5. Opposition to militarism and empire

Many anarchists criticize the U.S. state for maintaining a large military, foreign interventions, surveillance programs, and defense contracting systems. They argue that centralized states tend toward militarism because they compete for territory, resources, and geopolitical power.

A stateless society, in this view, could:

  • Reduce or eliminate large standing armies.
  • Prevent wars driven by state interests.
  • End military-industrial profiteering.
  • Shift resources from warfare to human needs.
  • Encourage international solidarity among people rather than rivalry among governments.

For anti-war anarchists, dismantling state power is connected to ending imperialism and militarized nationalism.

6. Economic alternatives to corporate capitalism

Not all anarchists are anti-market, but many oppose both state socialism and corporate capitalism. They argue that capitalism as it exists in the U.S. depends heavily on state enforcement of property rules, subsidies, patents, bailouts, policing, and corporate privileges.

Different anarchist schools propose different alternatives:

  • Anarcho-communists favor shared ownership and distribution according to need.
  • Anarcho-syndicalists favor worker-run unions and federated cooperatives.
  • Mutualists favor markets without state-backed monopolies, landlords, or corporate privilege.
  • Agorists and market anarchists favor voluntary exchange outside state control.

Despite differences, many agree that economic life should be less hierarchical and more voluntary.

7. Criminal justice and policing reform

Anarchists often argue that state policing and prisons produce violence, racial inequality, and social control rather than genuine safety.

They propose alternatives such as:

  • Community-based conflict mediation.
  • Restorative justice processes.
  • De-escalation teams.
  • Mental health crisis response.
  • Survivor-centered accountability.
  • Prevention through housing, healthcare, education, and social support.

The supposed benefit is a society focused less on punishment and more on reducing harm at its roots.

8. Stronger civic responsibility

Critics sometimes say that without government, no one would take responsibility for public goods. Anarchists respond that the state often encourages passivity by making people dependent on distant institutions.

They argue that stateless organization could encourage people to:

  • Participate directly in community decisions.
  • Build local support networks.
  • Share resources.
  • Resolve conflicts collectively.
  • Take responsibility for common needs rather than delegating everything to politicians.

In this sense, anarchism is presented not as “no organization,” but as self-organization.

Important caveat

These are the arguments made by proponents, not universally accepted conclusions. Critics argue that a stateless society could face serious problems, including defense, dispute resolution, infrastructure coordination, inequality, public health, and protection against violent groups. Anarchists respond with various models, but there is no single agreed blueprint.

In short, supporters believe a stateless anarchist society would replace coercive centralized government with voluntary, decentralized, cooperative institutions. They argue this could expand personal freedom, reduce corruption by dispersing power, and encourage people to collaborate directly rather than through imposed state authority.

Introduction

This is the foundational insight of anarchism: the state is not a unique moral entity exempt from the ethical standards we apply to individuals. Power Corrupts Because Power Is the Problem

Defenders of government often argue that with the right people, the right laws, and the right checks and balances, state power can be wielded justly. Every government, including the American one, rests on a single ugly premise: it claims the exclusive right to initiate violence against peaceful individuals within a given territory. You may not refuse its “services.” You may not opt out of its edicts. You may not keep the full product of your labor. Try it, and men with guns will come. This is not hyperbole; it is the literal operation of the tax code, regulatory state, drug laws, gun control, eminent domain, and conscription.

Murray Rothbard was correct: taxation is theft. It differs from private theft only in the scale of the perpetrator and the number of people who have been conditioned to call it moral. Once this foundational act of aggression is accepted, every other atrocity follows logically. The state does not “protect” rights; it systematically violates them while selling protection from the very threats it amplifies or creates.

The U.S. Constitution, often treated as a sacred limiting document, has failed spectacularly at its stated purpose. It was a coup against the more decentralized Articles of Confederation, and from the beginning it contained the seeds of its own expansion. The document that was supposed to create a government of enumerated powers has produced a regulatory octopus that claims authority over everything from the light bulbs in your home to the carbon dioxide you exhale. No piece of parchment can restrain an institution that writes, interprets, and enforces its own rules.

A Record of Corruption, Failure, and Moral Bankruptcy

The empirical case against the federal government is overwhelming. It has:

  • Waged perpetual wars, killing millions and bankrupting the nation, often on false pretenses.
  • Created the most expensive and least effective healthcare system in the developed world through massive intervention.
  • Engineered financial crises through central banking and favoritism toward politically connected firms.
  • Built the largest prison system on earth, disproportionately destroying the lives of the poor and minorities through the war on drugs.
  • Engaged in mass surveillance of its own citizens while lecturing the world about freedom.
  • Run trillion-dollar deficits for decades with no accountability, saddling future generations with debt for benefits enjoyed by current voters and special interests.

These are not bugs. They are features of any monopoly that faces no real competition and can print money and jail dissenters. Politicians do not fail because they are the wrong people. They fail because the incentive structure—concentrated benefits, dispersed costs, short time horizons, and the ability to use force—makes failure and corruption rational.

The idea that “we are the government” is a dangerous fiction. A handful of elites in Washington, revolving door bureaucrats, intelligence agencies, military contractors, and favored corporations make decisions that affect 330 million people. The average citizen has approximately the same influence over federal policy as a peasant had over the court of Louis XIV. Democracy is not liberty; it is the ritualized transfer of coercion from one faction to another every few years.

The Superiority of Voluntary Cooperation

A stateless society is not a utopia without rules or order. It is a society in which all rules and all order emerge from voluntary consent and reputation, backed by the right of self-defense and free association.

Private property, contracts, and the non-aggression principle provide the ethical foundation. Dispute resolution would be handled by competing private arbitrators and courts chosen for their reputation for fairness and efficiency—exactly as much of commercial arbitration already works today. Security would be provided by insurance companies and private defense agencies that compete on price and effectiveness rather than relying on a monopolist that fails to prevent crime while brutalizing the innocent. Roads, infrastructure, and public goods would be supplied by private owners, user fees, and voluntary communities, as they largely were before heavy federal involvement.

History and economics both support this. Mutual aid societies in the 19th and early 20th centuries provided welfare, insurance, and community support far more effectively and humanely than later state bureaucracies. The free market has consistently solved coordination problems that governments claimed were impossible. The internet itself developed largely outside heavy regulation and shows the power of spontaneous order. Even “national defense” against foreign invasion becomes far less necessary when there is no central state to conquer, tax, or control—and when an armed, free population makes occupation prohibitively expensive.

Human beings are capable of cooperation, charity, trade, and moral behavior without a gun pointed at them. Indeed, most of the good in the world—family, friendship, commerce, science, art—already operates on voluntary principles. The state is the outlier, not the foundation.

Addressing the Fear of Freedom

Critics claim anarchy equals chaos. This confuses the absence of rulers with the absence of rules. Dissolution does not require violent revolution. It requires the steady, deliberate withdrawal of consent and the building of parallel institutions. Educate people in the true nature of the state. The United States federal government is not reformable. It is not redeemable. It is a machine for converting human liberty and productivity into power, war, and bureaucracy. The only consistent position for anyone who values individual liberty is to demand its abolition root and branch.

It will eliminate the systematic, legalized initiation of violence that characterizes every state. It will allow genuine communities, genuine markets, and genuine moral agency to flourish. The experiment in limited constitutional government has run its course and failed. The next step in human political evolution is the rejection of the very concept of legitimate authority to rule others without consent.

The time has come to dissolve the United States federal government and embrace the beautiful, challenging, moral reality of freedom. The state is the enemy of the good. Let it go.

The future belongs to those brave enough to live without masters.

The Case for a Stateless America: Replacing Federal Authority with Voluntary Cooperation, Liberty, and Mutual Aid

I. Introduction – Why Question the State?

For more than two centuries the United States has been synonymous with “government of the people, by the people, for the people.” Yet the lived experience of millions of Americans tells a different story: a labyrinth of regulations that stifle entrepreneurship, a military‑industrial complex that consumes a disproportionate share of the national budget, a tax system that punishes productivity, and a political class that routinely trades public trust for private gain. By dismantling the centralized state, Americans can reclaim the autonomy promised by the founding ideals, foster resilient local communities, and unleash the creative, cooperative energies that have historically driven human progress.

II. The State as an Inherently Coercive and Corrupt Entity

A. The Monopoly on Violence

At its core, the state claims a monopoly on legitimate violence. Taxation, conscription, police enforcement, and regulatory penalties are all backed by the threat of force. This monopoly is not a neutral tool; it is a structural incentive for abuse. When an entity can compel obedience through coercion, it inevitably attracts those who seek power for its own sake. History—from the Roman Empire to modern authoritarian regimes—demonstrates that concentrated coercive power breeds corruption, surveillance, and the erosion of civil liberties.

B. The “Public Good” Myth

Proponents of the state argue that it provides essential services (defense, infrastructure, social safety nets) that would otherwise be under‑provided by the market. Yet empirical evidence shows that many of these services are delivered more efficiently, equitably, and innovatively by decentralized, voluntary arrangements. Public schooling, for instance, has produced stagnant outcomes despite skyrocketing spending, while community‑run learning cooperatives and online platforms have demonstrated higher student engagement and adaptability.

C. Capture by Special Interests

The federal government’s regulatory apparatus is a magnet for regulatory capture. Corporations, unions, and ideological groups spend billions lobbying to shape rules that protect their interests at the expense of ordinary citizens. The revolving door between regulators and the industries they oversee ensures that policy serves the powerful rather than the public. This systemic corruption undermines any claim that the state acts as an impartial guardian of the common good.

D. Moral Hazard and the Erosion of Personal Responsibility

When the state promises to solve every problem—healthcare, retirement, disaster relief—it creates a moral hazard: individuals and communities become dependent on distant bureaucracies, diminishing the incentives for self‑reliance, mutual aid, and local problem‑solving. The result is a populace less equipped to handle crises, more vulnerable to political manipulation, and less capable of exercising the autonomy that a free society demands.

III. Philosophical Foundations for a Stateless Society

A. Classical Liberalism and Natural Rights

The American founding was steeped in the ideas of John Locke, Adam Smith, and the Enlightenment thinkers who held that rights are inherent, not granted by government. Locke’s “life, liberty, and estate” are pre‑political; the state’s only legitimate function is to protect those rights. When the state exceeds this narrow mandate, it violates the very principles it was created to uphold.

B. Anarchist Thought: From Proudhon to Rothbard

Modern libertarian anarchism draws on a rich intellectual tradition. Pierre‑Joseph Proudhon declared “property is theft” when it is enforced by the state, while Murray Rothbard argued that a free market can provide law, security, and dispute resolution without a monopoly state. These thinkers demonstrate that voluntary exchange and private property can generate order without coercion.

C. Spontaneous Order and Polycentric Governance

F.A. Hayek’s concept of spontaneous order shows that complex, beneficial patterns can arise from decentralized decision‑making. Polycentric governance—multiple, overlapping legal and service providers competing for citizens’ approval—produces more adaptive, responsive institutions than a single, monolithic state.

IV. A Vision of a Stateless America

A. Voluntary Communities and Mutual Aid

Imagine a nation where neighborhoods, towns, and regions form voluntary associations that provide the services historically monopolized by the federal government. Community land trusts, cooperative housing, and mutual‑aid networks would ensure that basic needs—food, shelter, health care—are met through reciprocal support rather than forced taxation.

B. Market‑Based Law and Dispute Resolution

In place of a centralized judiciary, private arbitration firms and community courts would adjudicate disputes based on agreed‑upon contracts and customary law. Reputation systems, transparent rating mechanisms, and the threat of ostracism would enforce agreements, providing a robust alternative to state‑backed coercion.

The raiding of a family home at dawn, the seizure of assets without trial, the forced conscription of young men to fight in distant wars—these are not scenes from a dystopian novel but the daily realities under the United States federal government. The Inherent Coercion of State Power

The state, by definition, claims the right to initiate force against its subjects. Through taxation, regulation, and policing, it compels compliance under threat of violence—a system antithetical to human dignity. The U.S. government exemplifies this coercion: federal agencies like the IRS criminalize refusal to pay taxes, while police forces routinely escalate violence against marginalized communities. Historically, state power has enforced slavery, segregation, and imperialism, demonstrating that centralized authority inevitably serves the interests of the powerful. Beyond coercion, the federal government is a bastion of inefficiency and corruption. Trillions of dollars are wasted on bloated military-industrial complexes, while programs like the Federal Reserve enable Wall Street bailouts that deepen inequality. Regulatory agencies, captured by corporate interests, create barriers to entry that stifle innovation and entrench monopolies. Even well-intentioned policies, such as welfare programs, are laden with bureaucratic red tape that diverts resources from those in need. The state’s monopoly on force also breeds crony capitalism, where politicians trade favors for campaign donations. This cycle of graft and waste is not an anomaly but a predictable outcome of concentrated power. As Mikhail Bakunin noted, “The state is the worst form of human association,” precisely because it concentrates authority in the hands of the few.

Voluntary Cooperation: The Alternative to Coercion

A stateless society, grounded in anarchism, replaces hierarchy with horizontal networks of voluntary association. Imagine a world where roads are maintained by toll-based cooperatives, education is funded through community-supported schools, and defense is provided by competing private agencies incentivized to protect customers without coercion. History offers glimpses of this potential: medieval guilds fostered innovation through mutual aid, while modern cooperatives like the Mondragon Corporation in Spain demonstrate the efficacy of worker-owned enterprises. Technological advancements—from decentralized cryptocurrencies to open-source software—prove that complex systems can thrive without central control. In a crisis like the COVID-19 pandemic, grassroots mutual aid groups, not federal agencies, provided timely relief, illustrating the power of community-driven solutions.

Skeptics argue that a stateless society would descend into chaos. Yet, without a monopoly on violence, individuals and communities have every incentive to cooperate. Private defense firms would compete to offer affordable protection, reducing crime through market competition rather than state-enforced monopolies. As for public goods, voluntary mechanisms can suffice: toll roads fund infrastructure, subscription-based services deliver healthcare, and local communities collectively manage environmental resources. Transnational issues, such as climate change, could be tackled through international agreements among consenting nations or grassroots coalitions. Anarchist societies, like the Revolutionary Catalonia during the Spanish Civil War, briefly demonstrated functional stateless regions with robust economies and minimal violence—proof that cooperation, not coercion, is humanity’s natural state.

At its core, anarchism is a philosophy of consent. It rejects the notion that any individual or group should impose their will on others. In a stateless world, every interaction is voluntary: you choose your community, your work, and your associations. This principle upholds the inherent dignity of the individual, allowing marginalized groups—racial minorities, women, LGBTQ+ communities—to escape the systemic oppression perpetuated by hierarchical states. Decentralized power structures also prevent the concentration of identity-based hierarchies, fostering inclusive, participatory decision-making. As Peter Kropotkin argued, humanity’s survival depends on mutual aid, not state-enforced conformity. Anarchism aligns with this truth, prioritizing empathy, solidarity, and the right to opt out of oppressive systems.

Transitioning to a stateless society requires bold, incremental steps. We must decentralize power by reducing federal authority, empowering local governments, and funding community-based initiatives. Educational campaigns can cultivate a culture of self-reliance and voluntary cooperation, while technological tools—blockchain for transparent transactions, encrypted communication for organizing—can facilitate decentralized governance. Grassroots movements, from worker cooperatives to neighborhood mutual aid networks, can gradually replace state functions. The goal is not utopian chaos but a society where freedom is not a privilege granted by rulers but a birthright protected by the absence of rulers.

Conclusion: Embrace the Future of Freedom

The U.S. federal government, with its legacy of violence and corruption, has failed its people. Its continued existence hinges on the myth that coercion is necessary for order—a myth debunked by history and human ingenuity. A stateless, anarchist society offers not just an alternative but a moral imperative: to live in a world where every individual is sovereign, every interaction consensual, and every community free to chart its own path. The choice is stark: cling to a system that treats citizens as subjects, or courageously build a future where liberty is the foundation, not the exception. The time for revolution is now.
